readings.title: Meditations
readings.historical_context: Private philosophical notes by the Roman emperor Marcus Aurelius, shaped by Stoic practice.
readings.why_read_it: Direct access to Roman Stoic self-examination and response discipline.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not a modern therapy manual and not an Eastern philosophical text.
interpretive_cautions: Historical translation language can sound archaic.
Read individual entries within Stoic ethical context rather than as isolated motivational slogans.
readings.translation_notes: George Long is public domain and historically important; modern translations may be more readable but require separate rights handling.
readings.bibliographic_citation: Marcus Aurelius. Meditations. Translated by George Long. 1862.
readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for Meditations

readings.title: Discourses and Selected Writings
readings.edition: Penguin Classics paperback; includes the Enchiridion
readings.historical_context: A compact handbook based on Epictetus's Stoic teaching.
readings.why_read_it: One of the clearest starting points for the Stoic distinction between what is up to us and what is not.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not a promise that circumstances are controllable.
interpretive_cautions: Control-language is often better read as what is 'up to us' rather than total control.
readings.translation_notes: George Long's translation is public domain.
readings.bibliographic_citation: Epictetus. Discourses and Enchiridion. Translated by George Long.
readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for Discourses and Selected Writings

readings.title: Letters from a Stoic
readings.historical_context: Philosophical letters on practical Stoic ethics.
readings.why_read_it: Broad practical coverage and a more relational voice than a short handbook.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not a single systematic textbook.
interpretive_cautions: Individual letters address specific rhetorical contexts.
readings.translation_notes: Early Gummere volumes are public-domain in the U.S.; jurisdiction review still matters internationally.
readings.bibliographic_citation: Seneca. Moral Letters to Lucilius. Translated by Richard M. Gummere.
readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for Letters from a Stoic

readings.title: The Dhammapada
readings.historical_context: Verse collection in the Pali Canon.
readings.why_read_it: Accessible entry point into early Buddhist ethical and contemplative themes.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not a complete summary of all Buddhist schools.
interpretive_cautions: Müller's Victorian vocabulary is dated.
Do not read 'self' terminology through later Hindu atman concepts.
readings.translation_notes: Public-domain translation useful for provenance; compare terminology with modern scholarship.
readings.bibliographic_citation: Dhammapada. Translated by F. Max Müller. 1881.
readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for The Dhammapada

readings.title: The Suttanipāta
readings.edition: An Ancient Collection of the Buddha's Discourses and Its Canonical Commentaries
readings.historical_context: Early collection of Buddhist discourses and verses.
readings.why_read_it: Useful for seeing early Buddhist themes before later school-specific developments.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not a universal endorsement of social withdrawal.
interpretive_cautions: Renunciant solitude should not be generalized into advice for ordinary loneliness.
readings.translation_notes: Historical public-domain translation; use modern scholarship for interpretation.
readings.bibliographic_citation: Sutta-Nipata. Translated by Viggo Fausböll. 1881.
readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for The Suttanipāta

readings.title: The Gateless Gate
readings.author_or_attributed_author: Wumen Huikai (Mumon); commentary by Koun Yamada

readings.historical_context: Collection of forty-eight/forty-nine koan cases and commentary in the Chan/Zen tradition.
readings.why_read_it: A primary taste of koan literature when approached in its practice context.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not a book of riddles whose literal solutions provide mental-health advice.
interpretive_cautions: Paradoxical material should not be used to destabilize reality testing.

readings.bibliographic_citation: Wumen Huikai. The Gateless Gate. Translation by Nyogen Senzaki, 1934.

readings.title: The Bhagavad Gita
readings.historical_context: Dialogue between Arjuna and Krishna embedded in the Mahabharata, with multiple philosophical and devotional strands.
readings.why_read_it: Central source for Indian discussions of action, duty, attachment to outcomes, and liberation.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not a single-school summary of all Hindu philosophy.
interpretive_cautions: Do not flatten its metaphysics into generic mindfulness.
Historical battlefield framing requires contextual reading.
readings.translation_notes: Arnold is poetic and public domain; modern scholarly translations may be more literal but are generally copyrighted.
readings.bibliographic_citation: Bhagavad Gita. Translated by Sir Edwin Arnold as The Song Celestial. 1885.

readings.title: The Upanishads
readings.historical_context: A family of texts rather than one book; later Vedanta schools interpret them differently.
readings.why_read_it: Primary source for major Indian metaphysical questions about self, reality, and liberation.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not a single uniform doctrine and not identical with later Advaita Vedanta.
interpretive_cautions: Different Upanishads differ substantially.
Later schools should not be read back into every passage automatically.
readings.translation_notes: Müller is public domain but Victorian and philologically dated.
readings.bibliographic_citation: The Upanishads. Translated by F. Max Müller. Sacred Books of the East, Vols. 1 and 15.
readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for The Upanishads

readings.title: The Yoga Sutras of Patañjali
readings.edition: A New Edition, Translation, and Commentary
readings.historical_context: A concise sutra text of Classical Yoga that is usually read with commentary.
readings.why_read_it: Key source for practice, attention, non-attachment, and the analysis of afflictive patterns.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not a modern posture manual and not interchangeable with Vedanta.
interpretive_cautions: Sutras are compressed and commentary-dependent.

readings.bibliographic_citation: Patanjali. Yoga Sutras. Interpretation by Charles Johnston. 1912.

readings.title: Tao Te Ching
readings.historical_context: Composite classical Chinese text associated by tradition with Laozi.
readings.why_read_it: Short primary source for non-forcing, simplicity, perspective, and limits of control.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not a generic law-of-attraction or passivity manual.
interpretive_cautions: wu wei is not simply 'do nothing'.

readings.bibliographic_citation: The Texts of Taoism, Part I. Translated by James Legge. 1891.
readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for Tao Te Ching

readings.title: Zhuangzi: The Essential Writings
readings.historical_context: Layered classical text containing Inner, Outer, and Miscellaneous chapters.
readings.why_read_it: Rich source for perspective, transformation, non-forcing, and critique of rigid usefulness.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not proof that reality is unreal.
interpretive_cautions: Textual layers have different authorship histories.

readings.translation_notes: Legge is public domain; modern translations may better reflect current philology.
readings.bibliographic_citation: The Texts of Taoism, Parts I–II. Translated by James Legge. 1891.
readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for Zhuangzi: The Essential Writings

readings.title: Analects
readings.historical_context: Collected sayings and conversations associated with Confucius and disciples.
readings.why_read_it: Primary source for Confucian learning, relationship ethics, and cultivation.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not a productivity manual or a single authored philosophical treatise.

readings.translation_notes: Legge is public domain; modern translations offer different choices for key terms.
readings.bibliographic_citation: Confucius. Analects. Translated by James Legge.
readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for Analects

readings.title: Mengzi
readings.historical_context: Dialogues and arguments attributed to Mencius and his school.
readings.why_read_it: Deepens Confucian ideas of compassion, human nature, and moral development.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not the same position as every Confucian school.
interpretive_cautions: Mencius's account of human nature is contested by other Confucian thinkers.
readings.translation_notes: Historical translation is public domain; modern scholarship is useful for key-term nuance.
readings.bibliographic_citation: Mencius (Mengzi). English translation by James Legge; digital presentation via Chinese Text Project; contextual scholarship via Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for Mengzi

readings.title: The Four Books
readings.edition: The Basic Teachings of the Later Confucian Tradition
readings.historical_context: Classical texts later elevated within the Four Books tradition.
readings.why_read_it: Useful for seeing Confucian cultivation as a structured relation between self, relationships, and wider order.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not generic balance advice detached from Confucian ethical context.
interpretive_cautions: Later Neo-Confucian commentaries reshape their reception.
readings.bibliographic_citation: The Great Learning and Doctrine of the Mean. Translated by James Legge.
readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for The Four Books

readings.title: The Jains
readings.historical_context: A modern scholarly introduction to Jain history, doctrine, communities, scriptures, and practice.
readings.why_read_it: A serious book-length introduction that preserves Jainism's distinct history and doctrines instead of reducing it to a few slogans.
readings.what_it_is_not: Not a primary Jain scripture and not a generic guide to nonviolence.
interpretive_cautions: This is secondary scholarship; pair it with primary-source study when going deeper.

readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for The Jains

readings.editor: Brad Inwood and Lloyd P. Gerson
readings.historical_context: Diogenes Laertius preserves Epicurus's letters and doctrines.

readings.bibliographic_citation: Diogenes Laertius. Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers, Book X. Translated by C. D. Yonge.
readings.cover_image_alt: Book cover for The Epicurus Reader

readings.what_it_is_not: Not a comprehensive history of Zen and not a substitute for primary Chan/Zen texts.
